question: Can you walk me through the Linux filesystem hierarchy? What lives under /etc, /var, /usr, and /bin?
answer_html:
Linux organizes almost everything as files under a single root directory, /, rather than using drive letters. Each top-level directory has a conventional purpose defined by the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

  • /etc holds system-wide configuration files, mostly plain text (network config, service configs, cron tables).
  • /var holds variable data that changes at runtime: logs (/var/log), spool files, and caches.
  • /usr holds the bulk of installed user-space programs, libraries, and documentation — think of it as the read-only "system software" tree.
  • /bin and /sbin hold essential executables needed for basic system operation (on modern distros these are usually symlinked into /usr/bin and /usr/sbin).

Other important ones: /home for user data, /tmp for temporary files cleared on reboot, /opt for third-party self-contained applications, and /proc and /sys, which are virtual filesystems exposing kernel and process information rather than real files on disk.

Knowing this layout matters day to day: when a service misbehaves you check its config in /etc, its logs in /var/log, and its binary location with which or /usr/bin.

question: How does the Linux permissions model work — what do the rwx bits and octal notation actually mean?
answer_html:
Every file and directory has three permission sets: for the owner, the group, and others. Each set has three flags: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). Running ls -l shows this as a 10-character string like -rwxr-xr--, where the first character is the file type and the next nine are the three rwx triplets in order: owner, group, other.

For a regular file, read lets you view contents, write lets you modify it, and execute lets you run it as a program or script. For a directory, read lets you list its contents, write lets you create or delete entries inside it, and execute lets you cd into it or traverse it to reach files deeper in the path.

Octal notation compresses each triplet into a single digit by summing bit values: read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. So rwx = 7, rw- = 6, r-x = 5, and r-- = 4. A common permission like chmod 755 script.sh means owner gets rwx (7), group and others get r-x (5) — readable and runnable by everyone, but only the owner can edit it.

Ownership itself (which user and group a file belongs to) is separate from permissions and is changed with chown and chgrp; permissions are changed with chmod.

question: There are also special permission bits — sticky bit, SUID, and SGID. What do each of these do, and where would you actually see them used?
answer_html:
Beyond the standard rwx bits, Linux has three special permission bits that change how a file or directory behaves.

  • SUID (Set User ID, octal 4000): when set on an executable, the program runs with the privileges of the file's owner rather than the user who launched it. The classic example is /usr/bin/passwd, which is owned by root and has SUID set, so a normal user can update /etc/shadow (which they can't write directly) by running passwd.
  • SGID (Set Group ID, octal 2000): on an executable, it runs with the file's group privileges instead of the caller's. On a directory, it makes new files created inside inherit that directory's group instead of the creator's primary group — useful for shared team directories.
  • Sticky bit (octal 1000): on a directory, it restricts deletion so that only the file's owner (or root) can remove or rename files inside it, even if others have write access to the directory. /tmp is the textbook example — everyone can create files there, but users can't delete each other's files.

You'll see these as an extra letter in ls -l output: an s in the owner execute position for SUID, an s in the group execute position for SGID, and a t in the other execute position for the sticky bit (shown as rwxrwxrwt on /tmp). In octal, they're set as a fourth leading digit, e.g. chmod 4755 file for SUID, or chmod 1777 dir for a sticky, world-writable directory.

question: What exactly is a process, and how is it different from a program or a thread?
answer_html:
A program is a static file on disk — compiled code and data sitting there doing nothing. A process is that program loaded into memory and actually running: it has its own memory space, a process ID (PID), a parent process ID (PPID), open file descriptors, and a current execution state managed by the kernel scheduler.

You can run the same program multiple times and get multiple independent processes, each with its own memory and PID. Processes are isolated from each other by default; one process can't directly read another's memory without an explicit mechanism (like shared memory or IPC).

A thread is a unit of execution within a process. Multiple threads in the same process share that process's memory space and file descriptors, but each has its own stack and register state. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between than whole processes because there's no memory isolation to set up.

You can inspect running processes with ps aux or interactively with top/htop. Every process appears in the /proc/<pid> virtual filesystem, which is how tools like ps and top actually gather their data.

question: How do you manage services with systemd? Walk through starting, stopping, enabling, and checking the status of a unit.
answer_html:
systemd is the init system and service manager on most modern Linux distributions. It manages "units" — services, sockets, timers, mount points, and more — each defined by a unit file, typically under /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/.

  • systemctl start nginx starts the service immediately for the current session.
  • systemctl stop nginx stops it immediately.
  • systemctl restart nginx stops then starts it; systemctl reload nginx asks the service to reload its config without a full restart, if it supports that.
  • systemctl enable nginx creates a symlink so the service starts automatically on boot; it does not start it right now. systemctl enable --now nginx does both in one command.
  • systemctl disable nginx removes it from boot startup.
  • systemctl status nginx shows whether it's active, its main PID, recent log lines, and cgroup info — usually the first command you run when something's wrong.

After hand-editing a unit file, you need systemctl daemon-reload so systemd re-reads the definition before your next start/restart takes effect.

question: Explain process signals — what's the difference between SIGTERM, SIGKILL, and SIGHUP, and what happens if a process ignores them?
answer_html:
Signals are the kernel's way of notifying a process of an event, and a process can choose to handle, ignore, or be forcibly acted upon by most of them.

  • SIGTERM (15) is the default signal sent by kill and asks a process to terminate gracefully. A well-behaved process catches it, closes files/connections, and exits cleanly. This is what systemctl stop sends first.
  • SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored — the kernel terminates the process immediately with no cleanup. It's the last resort when a process won't respond to SIGTERM.
  • SIGHUP (1) originally meant "the controlling terminal hung up"; many daemons repurpose it as a signal to reload their configuration without restarting.

If a process ignores SIGTERM — maybe it's stuck in a blocking system call or has a bug in its signal handler — it simply keeps running. That's when you escalate: kill -TERM <pid>, wait a few seconds, then kill -KILL <pid> (equivalent to kill -9) if it hasn't exited. Because SIGKILL bypasses the process entirely, it also means the process can't release resources cleanly, which is why it's a last resort rather than a default.

question: What are zombie and orphan processes, and should you be worried if you see them in ps output?
answer_html:
A zombie process (shown as state Z in ps) is a process that has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't yet called wait() to read its exit status. The zombie holds essentially no resources besides that table entry — no memory, no open files — so a handful of short-lived zombies is normal and harmless. They disappear once the parent reaps them.

A problem arises when a parent process never reaps its children — a bug in the parent's code — causing zombies to accumulate indefinitely. Since you can't kill a zombie (it's already dead), the fix is to deal with the parent: restart it or fix the reaping logic.

An orphan process is different: it's a process whose parent died before the child did. The kernel re-parents orphans to PID 1 (or in cgroup-aware setups, to systemd or a subreaper), which will reap them properly when they exit. Orphans aren't inherently a problem — they're a normal part of process lifecycle, especially with backgrounded or daemonized processes.

In short: a few zombies briefly appearing is normal; a growing, persistent list of zombies points to a specific misbehaving parent process worth investigating.

question: What networking commands would you reach for to check a machine's IP configuration, see which process is listening on a port, or inspect DNS resolution order?
answer_html:
For interface and routing info, the modern tool is ip (from iproute2), replacing the older ifconfig/route: ip addr (or ip a) shows IP addresses on each interface, and ip route shows the routing table.

To see what's listening on which ports, use ss -tulpn: -t for TCP, -u for UDP, -l for listening sockets only, -p to show the owning process, and -n to skip DNS lookups and show numeric addresses/ports. This replaced the older netstat command on most modern distros. It's the go-to when you need to answer "is anything actually listening on port 8080, and which PID owns it?"

For capturing and inspecting live traffic, tcpdump lets you sniff packets on an interface, e.g. tcpdump -i eth0 port 443 to watch HTTPS traffic, useful for confirming whether packets are even arriving at the box.

DNS resolution order on Linux is controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf (the hosts: line), which typically says to check /etc/hosts first and then DNS. /etc/resolv.conf lists the actual DNS nameservers to query. Tools like dig or getent hosts <name> help verify what a lookup actually resolves to and via which path.

question: How do cron and systemd timers differ for scheduling recurring jobs, and where do you check logs for each?
answer_html:
cron is the traditional Unix job scheduler. Jobs are defined in crontabs — per-user via crontab -e, or system-wide in /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/ — using the familiar five-field time syntax (minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week). It's simple and universally understood, but has limited built-in logging and no easy way to express dependencies or track whether a job actually ran.

A systemd timer pairs a .timer unit with a corresponding .service unit: the timer defines when to fire (OnCalendar= for calendar-style schedules, or OnBootSec=/OnUnitActiveSec= for relative schedules), and the service defines what actually runs. You enable it like any unit: systemctl enable --now mybackup.timer. Timers integrate with the rest of systemd — you get dependency ordering, resource limits via the same cgroup controls as services, and automatic logging through journald.

For logs: cron job output typically needs to be redirected explicitly in the crontab entry (or check /var/log/cron / /var/log/syslog depending on distro), whereas a systemd timer's associated service logs automatically to the journal, viewable with journalctl -u mybackup.service. That built-in, queryable logging is one of the main reasons teams migrate recurring jobs from cron to systemd timers.

question: What triggers the Linux OOM killer, and how does it decide which process to kill?
answer_html:
The Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer is a kernel mechanism that steps in when the system is critically low on memory and can't satisfy an allocation request even after trying to reclaim caches and swap. Rather than letting the kernel itself crash, it kills a process to free memory and keep the system alive.

Each process has an oom_score, calculated primarily from how much memory it's using (with adjustments for things like process age and privileges), visible at /proc/<pid>/oom_score. The kernel picks the process with the highest score — generally the memory hog most likely to be the actual culprit — and sends it SIGKILL. You can influence this per-process via /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj, lowering it (even to -1000, which effectively exempts the process) to protect critical services, or raising it to make a process a preferred target.

After the fact, you confirm an OOM kill happened by checking the kernel log: dmesg or journalctl -k will show lines like "Out of memory: Killed process..." along with the memory stats at the time. This is a key thing to check whenever a process died with no application-level error and no exit code you'd expect from a graceful shutdown.

In containerized environments, the same mechanism applies within a cgroup's memory limit — a container hitting its memory limit gets a process inside it OOM-killed by the kernel, independent of the host's overall memory pressure.

question: A server reports the disk as full, but du shows plenty of space used. What's actually going on, and how do you diagnose it?
answer_html:
There are two independent resources on a filesystem: data blocks (actual file content) and inodes (metadata entries, one per file/directory, that track ownership, permissions, and where the data blocks live). A filesystem can run out of either one independently, and "disk full" errors look identical from the application's point of view either way.

First check actual space usage with df -h. If that shows real usage near 100%, you have a genuine space problem — track it down with du -sh /* narrowing into subdirectories to find the large consumer.

But if df -h shows space available yet writes still fail with "No space left on device," check inodes with df -i. If IUse% is at 100%, you've exhausted inodes — every one of the filesystem's fixed inode slots is used, even though the actual disk blocks aren't full. This commonly happens with workloads that create huge numbers of tiny files (session caches, mail queues, log rotation gone wrong) rather than a few large ones.

Another subtlety: a file can be deleted but still hold space if a process still has it open. du and df can then disagree because df reports actual block usage including those unlinked-but-open files, while directory listings show nothing. lsof +L1 (or lsof | grep deleted) finds processes holding deleted files open; restarting or having the process close the file descriptor reclaims the space.

question: A user says 'the server is slow.' Walk me through your triage process, and explain what load average actually tells you.
answer_html:
I'd start broad and narrow down, rather than guessing at a specific subsystem first.

1. Overall load and CPU: uptime or top shows the load average — three numbers representing the average count of processes in a runnable or uninterruptible-sleep state over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. A load average of 4 on a 4-core box means the CPUs are fully saturated on average; a load average of 4 on a 32-core box is barely a blip. Rising numbers across the three windows (e.g. 1-min much higher than 15-min) tell you the load just started spiking; falling numbers mean it's recovering. Note load average also counts processes blocked on disk I/O, not just CPU-bound ones, so a high load with low CPU usage in top points toward I/O rather than compute.

2. Memory: free -h or htop to check if memory is exhausted and the system is swapping heavily — swapping turns memory pressure into a CPU/disk problem too, since every swapped-out page access becomes a disk read.

3. Disk I/O: if load is high but CPU usage looks low, iostat -x 1 shows per-device utilization and %util/await times, revealing if a disk is saturated or slow to respond.

4. Narrow to the process: top/htop sorted by CPU or memory, or ps aux --sort=-%cpu, to identify the specific offending process, then check its logs (journalctl -u <service> or /var/log/) for what it was doing at that time.

5. Network, if the above look clean: ss -s for socket summary stats, or check if the app itself is waiting on a slow downstream dependency rather than the box being under local resource pressure at all.

The key habit is confirming which resource is actually constrained (CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network) before chasing an application-level explanation — the fix looks very different for each.
